items.originalTitle: How to Deal with Anxiety
items.author: Joan M. Cook
items.title: How to Deal with Anxiety
items.summary: —Creative Images Lab—Getty Images Hands down, anxiety is the most common mental health issue affecting Americans today. Over 19% of adults in the U.S. meet criteria for an anxiety disorder in any given year. Many often don’t recognize these difficulties, or mistake them for signs of a physical health condition. As a psychologist, I can tell you that worrying is a normal part of life. Occasionally, we all get a little nervous about something. We can fret that we blew a job interview or made a poor impression on a first date. We may feel on edge thinking about a big purchase we need to make and concerned about how we are going to pay for it. Many of us have concerns about money and finances, including how we are going to pay off a mortgage or a big debt. We may experience uneasiness about our relationships, including conflict with a partner or tension with an aging parent. We may be nervous about upcoming deadlines at work or national elections. Other times, our anxiety may be more free-floating, overly intense concerns latching on to any number of things. It’s hard to know how to safely stop the worry cycle, so we often, as humans, over-prepare, try to control a situation, or avoid it altogether. But when anxiety persists and gets worse over time, when it impairs our ability to function on the job or in the classroom, or our ability to connect with others, anxiety becomes problematic and potentially diagnosable. “Anxiety makes people’s lives smaller as they prune all the bits of their lives that lead to anxiety,” says Debra Kaysen , a psychologist and professor at Stanford University. “That works short-term, but long-term steals all the parts of life that give joy.” The great news is that there are effective treatments. Several free, reliable screens can help people do a self-assessment regarding whether they may meet criteria for an anxiety disorder. Though there are a range of anxiety disorders —including generalized anxiety, panic, phobias, and obsessive-compulsive disorder—most have similar underlying causes. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) can help to identify and manage the factors that contribute to anxiety. By learning to change unhelpful thought patterns, we can reduce the frequency and intensity of anxious symptoms. We can also learn techniques to regulate our anxiety and help us engage in effective problem-solving. That said, it isn’t always easy to get the help we need. There are a host of barriers, from financial, transportation, and scheduling to stigma, poor access, and limited availability. Anne Marie Albano , a psychologist and professor at Columbia University, has spent decades conducting research on and treating anxiety in children, adolescents, and young adults. Along with her colleagues, Albano developed several effective interventions, including Coaching Approach Behavior and Leading by Modeling (CALM) for families with young children to help them master circumstances that trigger intense discomfort, as well as the Launching Emerging Adults Program (LEAP), which centers on assisting individuals as they work through anxiety during the transition to adulthood. Albano recommends practicing breathing techniques to manage anxiety. “Close your eyes and focus on a quiet or pleasant scene in your mind. Breathe in slowly while counting to three, then pause a second, and then breathe out to the count of three. Breathing slowly and deeply, do this for ten repetitions,” she says. The benefit of this technique is that it’s endlessly versatile. “It’s a quick strategy that once learned, you can use with your eyes open and in any situation. Parents can even do this with their children to teach them belly breathing,” Albano explains. “Adults can use this before meetings or other emotionally challenging situations to regulate themselves and manage not just anxiety but other strong emotions.” In addition to breathing exercises, physical activity is one of the best ways to lessen anxiety for people of all ages. “Getting outside each day, rain or shine, and being physically active and social will build your natural resilience and coping skills. Walking, shooting hoops, yoga, swimming, and especially doing these things with other people will strengthen your physical capacity to manage stress and provide you with social networking and support from others,” Albano lists. Even just 10 or 15 minutes a day can help us feel more calm and capable. Even if, for whatever reason, someone is unable to access formal mental health services, there are things we can do to help ourselves with intense apprehension or looming thoughts of threat, trouble, or catastrophe. In my view, an excellent resource is the Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies , an interdisciplinary organization of professionals dedicated to the study of behavioral health. The website has research-based information in English and Spanish about anxiety disorders , treatments , and a therapist directory . Anxiety is common and treatable. The National Institute of Mental Health also offers a wealth of information on anxiety , including free digital brochures and fact sheets , updates from the latest research, and how to find help and support . Help is out there, and if you have persistent anxiety, rest assured you are not alone.

items.originalTitle: Adults are buying more toys than ever. You should too.
items.author: Jonquilyn Hill
items.title: Adults are buying more toys than ever. You should too.
items.summary: “When we're playing with a toy, we're often doing something we've never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes happen,” Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, tells Vox’s Explain It to Me podcast. | Chen Siyumeng/Xinhua via Getty Images Recently, I was out doing some window shopping with one of my friends. We checked out some of our usual places — a makeup store, a clothing store — but the place where my friend’s eyes really lit up was a toy store. There were floor-to-ceiling displays of Labubus and Funko Pops, Jellycats that looked like croissants, and just about every Hello Kitty product you could imagine. What really got my attention about the space was not the sheer volume of toys, but the lack of kids. It was mostly people our age, with the same excitement that I saw in my friend. This makes sense when you look at a breakdown of the current toy market: It’s an industry projected to be worth over $130 billion worldwide this year, and as of this summer, American adults with no kids bought more games and toys than households with children. There’s even a name for grownups who aren’t ready to put away the toybox: kidults. According to Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, there’s a reason for our enduring fondness for toys. “The drive to play is actually biologically hardwired into our subcortex,” she told Vox. “Because of that subcortical location, the drive to play actually lasts across the entire lifespan, which means that we’re never too old to play. But our society deeply misunderstands that. We’ve slowly started to take play away as we grow up, and yet that drive is still there.” So what does play actually do for our brains, and how can we add the playfulness of childhood back into our adult lives? We answer that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Sundstrom, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545. Adult consumers are making up the lion’s share of the toy industry now. What is happening in our adult brains when we play with toys? Neuroplasticity means that our brains can adapt across our entire lifespan. Some of the similar benefits that children have with playing with toys, we actually still have as adults. The primary reason is because of the hand-brain connection, which is essentially a two-way neurological highway. When we do fine motor movement while we’re playing with toys, it stimulates the brain regions that are responsible for our cognitive function, our emotion, and our focus. It activates these deep neural networks that go completely unused when we’re engaging in, say, passive screen time. When we’re playing with a toy, we’re often doing something we’ve never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes happen. That is actually stimulating new neural pathways in our brain that support our long-term cognitive health. The second big one is our amygdala, which is a key part of our emotional processing center in our brain, is relaxed in the state of play. A lot of us live in a stress response right now. Social media doesn’t really take us out of that stress response. It often leaves us feeling more stressed out or drained when we’re done. I absolutely have experienced that. But that’s not the case with the toys. When we engage in this play state with toys, our amygdala actually calms down. The amygdala is responsible for our stress response. So our stress, our anxiety, our emotional defensiveness are significantly reduced, and we enter that restorative state, which for a lot of us is really hard to access on the day-to-day. Toys are a pathway to helping us access that more relaxed emotional state based on the reactivity of our amygdala. When do we start being told that we’re too old for toys? What do we lose when we accept that? Sadly, I think we’re being told that we’re too old for toys starting quite early. Specifically, when we hit the teenage years, a lot of play is replaced with, “If this doesn’t have an immediate purpose for my future career, it’s not worth the time.” That free space to experiment, say, with Lego and even with collections and other things that stimulate our imagination and allow us to enter this world between imagination and reality, starts to slowly dwindle out, almost imperceptibly. Parents think that they’re doing their children a service by replacing that free play time with structured sports or structured activities. Unfortunately, what happens is, slowly, the intrinsic motivation to do something gets replaced with extrinsic motivation, which very quickly leads to burnout. It sounds like when we stop playing with toys, that’s when the optimization culture kicks in. Exactly. We see playing with toys as extra, as a hobby, as something that doesn’t have an immediate purpose toward helping us achieve whatever our goals are. And yet paradoxically, it’s one of the most productive things we can do. One of the things that I like to ask people is, “Where are you when you get your best ideas?” Now, the shower is the most common answer, but the second most common answer is when they’re playing with toys. You know how no one answers that question? “When I’m at my desk at 10 am answering emails.” The creative mind flourishes in the space in between, and the space in between is the time that is spent playing with toys. But until people see it like that, it becomes really hard to fit into the hustle culture and the grind of the daily schedule. How do we relearn how to play? “Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference.” The first step is to think back on our earliest memories of playing, because play is who we were before the world told us who we have to be. The second, which is a derivative of that, is understanding your own play style. For some people, building a Lego set is going to be totally playful. For other people it’s going to be a puzzle or it’s going to be a game night with a board game or a sports league. And third, this is not about adding more to our plate. Nobody has time for that. That’s so funny. My first thought is, “I need to put play on my to-do list.” And that is totally contradictory to the purpose of play! Here’s the good news: Even 30 seconds to five minutes a day makes a difference. You can put play objects and toys in visible places around your environment so that you reach for that instead of your phone. If you just crack the door open a little bit with those micro moments of play in your routine, your brain will automatically enjoy it and start looking for more opportunities to play. Just start really small and know that that’s enough. What do you think the world looks like when adults embrace that playful spirit more? The world looks more joyful. This isn’t all sunshine and rainbows, and play doesn’t take away from the hard things that it means to be human. Play is a healthy way to express those challenges and to express the full range of emotions. Play can look mellow and play can look lower-energy, but what it looks like is humans honoring what it means to be human and feeling more connected with your authentic self. When we’re more connected with our authentic self, we’re more easily able to connect with the people around us and establish meaningful relationships. So I see this as a tool for societal flourishing, specifically in a technologically dominated world.

items.originalTitle: What We Don’t Know About the Iran War
items.author: Pete Kiehart / Bloomberg / Getty
items.title: What We Don’t Know About the Iran War
items.summary: P resident Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have a ready answer to the question of how the nine-month conflict with Iran has gone: We won . But the administration has done just about everything in its power to obstruct scrutiny of that dubious claim, hiding from the public the full cost of the operation in both lives and money. When Senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat from Connecticut, headed to the Persian Gulf last month, he made what would once have been considered a routine request to visit Al Udeid, the giant U.S. air base outside the capital of Qatar that is home to the regional headquarters of Central Command. Typically, the base is home to 10,000 troops and more than 100 aircraft. Iran pounded it with air strikes soon after Trump launched the Iran war in February, but the conflict was largely paused when Murphy showed up. Murphy sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee, which must decide how the government spends taxpayer money. It’s the committee that has to sign off on expected funding requests to repair Al Udeid and other bases hit by Iranian attacks, as well as the extra $67 billion the administration has sought for war costs. Murphy requested a tour, a briefing, anything that could help him make an assessment of the damage and cost of repairs. The Pentagon said no. When Republican Senator Joni Ernst of Iowa, an Army veteran who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, made her own trip to the Gulf around the same time, the Defense Department told her that she would not be able to conduct base visits, a person familiar with the matter told me. Ernst’s office did not reply to a request for comment. Behind the rebuffs lies a decision made by Hegseth early in the war to discourage congressional travel to the region. The Pentagon couldn’t ban lawmakers from heading to the Middle East. But Hegseth instructed the Pentagon’s legislative office to “inform the appropriate congressional leadership that DoW support to congressional delegation visits will be unavailable,” according to a March 3 memo I reviewed. (DoW is an acronym for the Department of War, Hegseth’s preferred name for the Department of Defense.) To emphasize the point, the memo added: “No DoW support shall be made available for congressional travel to the USCENTCOM AOR without my approval.” (U.S. Central Command is in charge of war operations; AOR stands for “area of responsibility.”) Perhaps the edict made sense in the war’s earliest days. But the campaign had already been in limbo for many months by the time Murphy and Ernst made their requests. The policy remains in effect. Senators aren’t the only people being denied access. Early in the war, the U.S. military provided a drumbeat of information about how the war was going. But that information was highly selective: the Defense Department offered a tally of “targets struck” (13,000 in the initial weeks) and the hardware deployed. The Pentagon regularly turned down media requests for more detail, citing “operational security.” And it has allowed only a handful of reporters to embed with troops, far fewer than in previous wars. Hegseth and General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, also held sporadic press conferences at the start of the conflict, during which Hegseth detailed how much of Iran’s military had been destroyed. The secretary insisted that the U.S. military was being transparent and that anyone who thought otherwise was trying to attack the president or was being unpatriotic. (This was after he had severely restricted media access to the Pentagon and vowed to go after purported leaks.) But as the war ground on, the press conferences stopped. Hegseth hadn’t held one since early May until last week, when he used the occasion to argue against an effort to impeach him by a congressman of his own party. [ Read: The last days of the Pentagon press corps ] Although Congress and the public have continued to pose questions that are central to understanding the war, the administration has provided only inadequate answers. What exactly led to a U.S. strike on a school in Minab, Iran, on the first day of the war, killing more than 170 civilians? A targeting error was reportedly to blame, but a Centcom report on the incident has not been released, and Hegseth has never addressed the cause. How much damage have Iran’s strikes done to U.S. facilities in the Middle East? What little we know comes largely from photos taken by witnesses that were posted to social media, satellite images (many of them released by Iranian media), and outside estimates. What happened to U.S. citizens and government personnel in the region? We learned details of the hasty evacuation of military families from the giant Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain only when some of the evacuees claimed , months later, that the Pentagon had treated them poorly. What has the war done to the supply of air-defense missiles? The Trump administration has banned some news organizations from the White House, citing their reporting on the dramatic shortfalls, among other factors. How many times has Iran hit U.S. bases in the region? Some significant attacks have not been disclosed, including missile strikes on the air command center at Al Udeid or on a U.S. ship in the Strait of Hormuz, both of which were later reported by the media. What were the circumstances that caused the deaths of 23 American service members and injuries to more than 850 others? And is that casualty count even accurate? Trump is now considering resuming strikes on Iran in an attempt to head off the reconstitution of its nuclear and missile programs, despite the strong signal of disapproval that voters sent in the midterms. Plans for a renewed escalation are on his desk, and he has told Vice President Vance not to make any overtures to Tehran, saying the time for diplomacy is over. The information vacuum of the last nine months means that even as the president contemplates taking the nation back into conflict, we have a limited picture of what has already happened. H egseth’s disdain for the press and for engaging with Congress began long before the war. Before his 2025 confirmation hearings, he declined to hold customary meetings with most Democratic senators on the Senate Armed Services Committee. Once in office, he barred even very senior Pentagon officials from engaging Congress without authorization. Pentagon officials have provided a series of classified briefings on the Iran war for lawmakers. U.S. Central Command told me that it has engaged with them roughly 60 times this year, through testimony, briefings, and phone calls. But the flow of information has been restricted to partisan allies. Republican Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota this week criticized the Pentagon for excluding Democrats from classified briefings about threats while defense officials are asking Congress for new funding. The same has happened in the House. “Pretty tough to ask all of my colleagues to support that, if they’re not even invited in to hear the information in the first place,” Rounds told Hung Cao, Trump’s nominee to lead the Navy. Military officials have also limited disclosures to official government watchdogs. In a September report on the costs of the war, the Congressional Budget Office—Capitol Hill’s resident bean counter—was forced to piece together information, largely from public reporting, to estimate the value of lost equipment (at least $1.9 billion, it concluded) because the Pentagon didn’t respond to its requests for information. Pentagon officials have estimated the cost of the war’s operations and replacement of munitions at about $48 billion as of mid-November, but many people believe that the full tally is far higher. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, and several Senate colleagues complained last month that the Pentagon provided only a classified cost estimate that they were unable to share with the public. The State Department had no such qualms and disclosed its own estimate for the repair of U.S. diplomatic facilities in the region: about $184 million through the end of June. [ Read: How the U.S. squandered its strategic advantage ] The Pentagon has said it can’t provide a cost estimate for the damage because officials haven’t decided what and where to rebuild. A spokesperson for the Pentagon declined to provide an on-the-record comment for this story. Murphy told me he has been trying to fill in some of the information gaps. “How on earth could we make decisions that we are empowered by the Constitution to make about whether we fund war if we can’t see it?” he said during an event last month. Of course, there is always an element of political grandstanding to lawmaker trips. But lawmakers have asserted their prerogative to make fact-finding missions as part of the U.S. system of checks and balances. Some congressional staff members told me they understood the Pentagon would want to avoid diverting resources during an active fight. And one former Biden administration official told me that, early in the Ukraine war, the administration at times barred lawmakers from traveling to Kyiv. But the Pentagon ultimately relaxed the ban and made security arrangements to support lawmakers’ visits, even though the Ukraine war, unlike the Iran war, is not one where the U.S. has been a direct participant. Robert Wilkie, who served as the Pentagon’s top legislative-affairs official during the Iraq War, told me that Hegseth’s blanket ban on access for lawmakers marked a departure from a practice that dated to at least World War II. Military leaders may not have always loved the spectacle associated with those visits, but they knew such trips were an essential part of congressional oversight. They’re also a tool the military uses to persuade lawmakers to favor bigger budgets. As Wilkie put it, referring to the gun-slinging action hero of the 20th century: “The commanders understand that it’s ‘No bucks, no Buck Rogers.’” T he Pentagon’s disclosures about the war’s toll on military personnel have been limited and obscured by bureaucratic choices. A Pentagon-run website lists the deaths and injuries of service members for all major U.S. conflicts going back to World War I. But in July, four deaths and dozens of injuries disappeared from its totals for Operation Epic Fury, the military’s name for the Iran war. At first, the Pentagon blamed a “data disruption” and said that there was no effort to mask the true toll. Days later, the website was updated with a new category: “Overseas Operations.” The deaths and injuries that had disappeared reemerged under the new listing. Officials pointed to a letter Trump had sent to Congress claiming a new conflict with Iran had started on July 7. Some of the service members wounded in Iranian attacks have said that the military downplayed or dismissed their injuries. The Defense Department’s division of casualties into two categories makes it harder for the public to see the total toll. The Pentagon has defended the system’s accuracy despite what it has described as “website glitches.” [ Read: The Top Gun: Maverick theory of Pete Hegseth ] Hegseth has at times appeared dismissive of casualties. A drone attack in the opening days of the war killed six troops at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait. When reporters sought details, Hegseth accused the press of hyping the loss. “When a few drones get through or tragic things happen, it’s front-page news,” he told reporters at a news conference on March 4. “The press only wants to make the president look bad.” Congress’s new Democratic leaders can be expected to push the Pentagon on its handling of casualties when they take over early next year. Hegseth and Trump may want to portray the war as a victory already in hand. But the defense secretary still needs lawmakers on at least one front: money. In a video statement before the planned impeachment vote, Hegseth included a pitch for the administration’s $1.5 trillion military budget request and for tens of billions more to cover the already-sunk costs of the Iran war—whatever those really are.

items.originalTitle: A Movie About What Happens When the Party’s Over
items.author: A24
items.title: A Movie About What Happens When the Party’s Over
items.summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Fiza Kuzhiyil, an assistant editor on the Community team who works on Rabbithole , the magazine’s daily trivia game. Fiza has dedicated her year to a timeless read: Anna Karenina . She also enjoys the movie Club Kid , playing Overcooked 2 with her brother, and visiting the Rothko Chapel when she goes home to Houston. — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor The Culture Survey The last thing that made me cry: Club Kid —a touching story about what happens when the party is over. This film is the grown-up version of the only Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson movie I have ever seen: the 2007 Disney classic (at least in my household) The Game Plan . Rather than depicting the queer party scene as a hedonistic trap, Club Kid celebrates it as a source of real joy and community. This film feels like the Uber ride home after a party, so how could I—someone who cries at the end of a hangout because I’m so grateful for my friends—not leave in tears? The last thing that made me snort with laughter: Also Club Kid . If you’re as online as I am, you’ll roll your eyes at the meme-speak, but it’s impossible not to laugh when you get the references—the kind that make you feel seen, then immediately worried about your screen time. Best novel I’ve recently read: Instead of setting a numerical reading goal this year, a friend and I decided to commit to one great, long classic: Anna Karenina . When people ask me if I’ve read anything good recently, I almost always skip over it, not because it didn’t rank, but because what more is there to say than Anna Karenina is the best novel of all time? I can hardly add to what these 19th-century Russian characters have already described about the emotions that I also know—emotions so familiar, they transcend language. Reading it showed me how everyone who came before me has expressed the same thrills, fears, and heartbreaks that I have. The joy of experiencing this novel comes not from deep revelations of plot, but from immersing yourself in the lives of these characters; or, in Leo Tolstoy’s own words, “Pleasure lies not in discovering truth, but in seeking it.” A quiet song that I love, and a loud song that I love: “Oh, What a World,” by Kacey Musgraves is always my reminder to be quiet, listen to the world, and take note of my senses. Its counter in my life is the rhapsodic “Trinidad,” by Geese, which is my reminder to accept the tension buzzing among everything I see, hear, and touch. That being said, my loved ones don’t find it amusing when I let go of these tensions by randomly yelling the lyrics to this song (“THERE’S A BOMB IN MY CAR”). A musical artist who means a lot to me: Lorde’s four-year music-release cycles have aligned perfectly with major chapters of my life. I made a big cross-country move listening to Pure Heroine , spent late nights in high school with Melodrama , emerged from the pandemic bubble with Solar Power , and started my first years out of college with Virgin . I saw her three times on her most recent tour, and each time, she sang and spoke about the same themes many artists do— love, loss, youth, autonomy —but the rawness and precision in her delivery has always affected me a step above the others. A painting, sculpture, or other piece of visual art that I cherish: The Rothko Chapel in Houston, both a nondenominational meditative space and an art exhibition, is the only place of worship I visit regularly. I was lucky to have lived on the same street as the chapel for some time. Whenever I feel disoriented or untethered, a quiet moment with the blackout triptychs feels baptismal. Something I recently revisited: My Beatles album ranking—I was always a Sgt. Pepper girl, but I think I’m entering a Rubber Soul time of my life. A piece of journalism that recently changed my perspective on a topic: Some of my D.C. friends call me the one-woman Houston Department of Tourism—which is to say that I won’t shut up about Houston or Texas. Inevitably, non-Texans ask me about Buc-ee’s, the behemoth of a gas station. For a while, its outsize Texas-ness felt like a point of cultural pride; I liked being asked about it. But Forrest Wilder’s essay in The Baffler about the company’s water-rights battles and the cost taxpayers incur for its expansion changed the way I felt about letting Buc-ee’s represent me or my state. I may still wear my beaver-printed running shorts, but I think differently about allowing a corporation to serve as a cultural marker. My favorite way of wasting time on my phone: I am delighted by the recent obsession with browser games among my friends. Krillion rewards obscure and rare answers with more points, which, frankly, panders well to my uniqueness complex. I also spend too much time playing Catfishing , but I consider it “research” for the trivia questions I write for The Atlantic ’s Rabbithole game (shameless plug). Something delightful introduced to me by a kid in my life: Overcooked 2 . I don’t know if I’d call the game itself delightful, because I often take breaks so as to not get too angry, but I am delighted by how my little brother and I are forced to communicate better when we play it. I once preferred the soothing music and satisfying chopping of Cooking Mama on Nintendo DS, but my brother put me on to the new wave of cooking games: cooperative, stressful, and fast-paced. A major perk of our large sibling age gap is that our daily functions rarely overlap, so we have few reasons to get mad at each other. But through Overcooked , we have finally found a way. Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic : Ian Bogost: What on earth is going on? The real reason Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond Maxwell Taylor Kennedy: Trump’s arch must be stopped. The Week Ahead Focker-in-Law , a new installment in the Meet the Parents comedy franchise, starring Robert De Niro and Ariana Grande (in theaters Wednesday) Blade Runner 2099 , a sci-fi series set in the dystopian world of the Blade Runner 2049 film, 50 years later (streaming Wednesday on Prime Video) Long Wave , a novel by Daisy Johnson about three generations of women and the family secrets that begin to unravel when a toddler is found alone on a remote island (out Tuesday) Essay Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic The Least Productive Day of the Year By Sophia Nguyen Kelsey Rogers, a 26-year-old working in construction in San Antonio, Texas, didn’t want to tell her boss why she was asking for time off. First, she chalked it up to “personal reasons.” Then she said her birthday was coming up. But eventually, she came clean: She wanted to play Grand Theft Auto VI right when the game dropped, on November 19. Rogers had big plans—decorating with neon lights, stocking up on energy drinks, adorning those drinks with little paper umbrellas. She and her fiancé were going to play until their eyes gave out. She didn’t have to worry: Her boss admitted that he was taking time off for the same reason. “I don’t think the company’s even going to be up and running for probably two or three days,” Rogers told me. If you’ve got a metal roof that needs replacing in south-central Texas, it just might have to wait. Read the full article. More in Culture Anna Holmes: ChatGPT analyzed 32,245 of my text messages. items.originalTitle: Independent audit suggests several changes to Wisconsin school district report cards
items.author: Corrinne Hess / WPR
items.title: Independent audit suggests several changes to Wisconsin school district report cards
items.summary: Reading Time: 3 minutes An independent audit is calling for changes in Wisconsin’s school report cards, saying they fall short of providing school performance information required by statute. The Legislative Audit Bureau, or LAB, issued a 146-page report Friday reviewing school report cards from 2022 through 2025 for public, charter and private schools. The audit was commissioned by the Republican-led Joint Legislative Audit Committee in February 2025 after DPI changed how the report cards are scored. LAB made 13 recommendations to DPI and suggested the department report to the Joint Legislative Audit Committee by March 30, 2027 on efforts to implement all of the recommendations. After receiving the report, Sen. Eric Wimberger, R-Gillett, and Rep. Robert Wittke, R-Caledonia, who chair the audit committee, said “DPI unilaterally turned school report cards into an untrustworthy sham.” “Accountability is not optional,” Wittke said in a statement. “The Department of Public Instruction must demonstrate that it is putting Wisconsin students, families, and schools ahead of politics and bureaucracy.” State Superintendent Jill Underly said it is “notable” that the audit is being released the same week school district report cards were issued after months of silence from LAB. “Let’s be clear: Our job at the DPI is to do what’s best for Wisconsin’s kids and families. The Legislative Audit Bureau’s job is to conduct objective, fact-based audits, and not play politics,” Underly said in a statement. “This audit offers nothing new,” Underly continued. “The DPI has been transparent throughout this process, participated in multiple public legislative hearings on these issues, and repeatedly answered questions about our work. Instead of providing meaningful new information and recommendations, the audit makes factually incorrect assertions, goes beyond the scope of its review, and reads like a continuation of last legislative session’s partisan political theater rather than a review conducted in good faith.” Lowest performing schools not receiving intervention On Tuesday, 95% of Wisconsin public school districts were ranked with three, four or five stars. Those rankings reflect meeting, exceeding or significantly exceeding expectations. School report cards look at four priority areas for three school years: achievement, growth, target group outcomes and on-track to graduation. At the same time, test scores released in October showed 48% of students in grades three through 11 were proficient or above in reading while about 49% were proficient or above in math. Part of the reason for this discrepancy is DPI weighs student achievement and growth more than student performance in calculating overall scores in low income districts. This methodology was approved by a GOP-led state Legislature and signed into law by former Gov. Scott Walker. Critics of the state report card say methodology makes it impossible for parents to make apples-to-apples comparisons between districts across the state. In 2021, a bill was introduced that would have given all four priority areas equal weight. Gov. Tony Evers vetoed the bill. In his veto message, Evers said he objected to the Legislature’s “continued efforts to politicize our schools and our classrooms.” Criticism for state report cards grew louder in 2024, when DPI rolled out new testing standards and updated the “cut scores ,” which determine where the schools and districts fall on the star scale. At the time, Underly said the updates were needed to keep pace with changes to performance measures. Republicans and outside conservative groups, including the Wisconsin Institute for Law and Liberty and Institute for Reforming Government, have continued to argue the changes lowered standards. Wimberger said the audit shows DPI “circumvented statutes and lowered cut scores so that otherwise failing schools appear to be on track.” While the audit released Friday does not specifically say that DPI lowered standards, it found that DPI’s assessment process is not creating conditions for intervention when schools are meeting minimal performance standards. The percentage of schools meeting, exceeding, or significantly exceeding expectations increased from school year 2022-2023 to school year 2024-2025, and the percentage of schools meeting few expectations or failing to meet expectations decreased from school year 2022-2023 to school year 2024-2025, according to the audit. The school performance category assigned to most schools and school districts did not change from school year 2023-2024 to school year 2024-2025. However, 20.2% of schools and 21% of school districts moved up one school performance category during that time, the audit found. The audit also found DPI should have released written policies to all stakeholders about testing changes. The audit says the department did not solicit feedback broadly from educators or members of the public before making changes. “Although DPI indicated it received informal feedback from stakeholders about changing assessment cut scores through ad hoc conversations and discussions during meetings and presentations, DPI was unable to provide documentation of the feedback it received or how it used the feedback to inform the changes it made,” the audit found. This story was originally published by WPR . items.summary: It has been difficult in recent days to tune to a television news show and not see Scott Colom or at least people talking about Scott Colom. He has become sort of a national sensation – the next big thing for political nerds and perhaps even for many who take a more casual interest in politics. In the Nov. 3 midterm election, Colom, a Democratic district attorney from the Lowndes County area, upset Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become the first Black person elected through popular vote to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi. The watershed election has to be viewed against the historical backdrop of Mississippi’s sordid racist history. Regardless of one’s political views, it could be argued that Colom’s victory provides Mississippi a good dose of needed redemption. Mississippi is only the third state from the footprint of the old Confederacy – and all of the lingering segregation and racism that followed the downfall of the Confederacy – to have elected a Black person to the United States Senate. South Carolina elected Republican Tim Scott in 2012, and Georgia elected Democrat Raphael Warnock in 2020. Perhaps more impressive in terms of Colom’s accomplishment is that only nine Black people before this year have ever been elected via popular vote to the United States Senate. Come January, Colom will join five other Black senators, including the aforementioned fellow Southerners, Warnock and Scott. Being sworn in with Colom will be Juliana Stratton, the second Black woman elected to the Senate from Illinois and the fifth Black woman ever elected to the upper chamber of Congress. Illinois has elected the most Black senators – three – and had another who was appointed to succeed Barack Obama after he was elected president. Only nine states – California, Delaware, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, South Carolina and now Mississippi – have elected Black senators. It is worth noting that a Mississippi native, Laphonza Butler , was appointed to fill one of California’s U.S. Senate seats in 2023 after the death of Sen. Dianne Feinstein. Butler service until December 2024 and did not seek election to the post. It is also worth noting that Mississippi was the only state after the Civil War during Reconstruction to have Black citizens serve in the U.S. Senate – Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce . They were selected by the state Legislature instead of via popular vote. Again, regardless of one’s politics, it is fair to say Mississippi is a trendsetter in this particular instance. But an important question for us here in Mississippi is: What took us so long to elect a Black person to a statewide office? Before Colom, Mississippi had not elected a Black person to statewide office since Reconstruction, despite currently having the largest percentage of Black residents in the country – around 38%. Mississippi has had some Black candidates get relatively close in statewide election efforts. In the 2003 race for state treasurer, Democrat Gary Anderson, who was the state fiscal officer under Gov. Ronnie Musgrove, garnered 46.6% of the vote in a losing effort against Republican Tate Reeves, a political unknown running his first campaign. In November 2018, former U.S. Agriculture Commissioner Mike Espy captured 46.4% of the vote in losing a special election to Hyde-Smith, who had been appointed by Gov. Phil Bryant earlier that year to serve temporarily after fellow Republican Thad Cochran retired. Hyde-Smith and Espy competed to fill the remaining years of Cochran’s term. Two years later when Hyde-Smith was running for a full six-year-term, Espy received 44.1% of the vote in a rematch. It should be pointed out that the 2020 election was a presidential year and the highest vote-total election in the state’s history. In that election, Espy captured nearly 100,000 more votes in a losing effort than Colom received in his recent winning effort. Election turnouts are normally much lower in midterm elections than in presidential elections. Mississippi is one of few states that elect a governor, other statewide offices and state legislators between the presidential and midterm elections. So, next year Mississippi will elect eight statewide officials, including for the open office of governor because Reeves cannot seek a third term. A big question now: Will another Black candidate replicate Scott Colom’s success to win a different statewide office?

items.originalTitle: Make America boring again
items.author: Vic Snyder
items.title: Make America boring again
items.summary: Ben Shapiro , the conservative commentator and movie maker, is not happy with today’s Republican Party and quite disappointed with where Donald Trump’s decisions have taken our country. He has not been reluctant to express his views. But at the end of a recent NPR interview, he was asked what advice he had for Democrats and what advice for Republicans. His answer, he said, was the same for both parties: the American people want normal. My guess is he means normal by the standards of the American people, not elected officials who won or survived an earthquake of an election. Here’s what I think normal looks like: less chaos. We used to call this business climate. Tariffs have a place in modern economies, but during the past two years Trump’s tariff policy has had the stability of a teenager crush. Trade agreements exist to give predictability for businesses, not to be ignored in some moment of anger or bewilderment. Confusion about America’s world leadership, the importance of NATO, and the threat of Russia to Europe and the world contributes to instability internationally. Second, the American people want a Congress that goes to work and works for them. Rep Jim Jordan ’s apparent belligerent intent as the new minority leader misses the potentially important role that minority members can play in shaping legislation. And Rep. Robert Garcia ’s repeated school-ground threat to his oversight targets to “lawyer up” misses several realities. The Trump family was born lawyered up, and does anyone doubt the likelihood that Trump’s pardons prior to leaving office will be broad? The American people want oversight that makes us a better country by improving law, improving transparency, and stopping corruption. Criminal referrals are important in congressional oversight, but Americans don’t want shows, particularly if they seem to be connected with campaign fundraising. I am tired of Rep Garcia’s fundraising requests. Third, how about a list of priorities that warrant oversight and change? Here’s a few. Tens of thousands of Americans are still recovering from natural disasters. Disasters are always in our future. What is the role of FEMA now and what will it be going forward? Can we return to a FEMA that has the confidence of the American people like we did with Arkansas’ James Lee Witt? For many areas of the country businesses depend on a strong tourist economy connected to our national parks and public lands. What is happening to the National Park System? Where is the funding going? Why is staffing inadequate? Have funds been diverted to weird projects in Washington, D.C.? With Democrats now in control, let’s find out the status of medical research, research that improves our health and drives a chunk of our economy. What have we lost and how much can be recovered from DOGE amateur-hour cuts? Have researchers been so intimidated they have been reluctant to talk candidly about the impact of funding cuts and what it means for the research infrastructure and the health of Americans? Why are health insurance rates increasing, and what can be done about it? Americans need financial stability for themselves, their children, and their small businesses. A strong rural America depends on strong rural hospitals with financial predictability. Normal governing should not fill every day with breaking news. It is work. I am confident there are many representatives and senators, new and old, many not in the news, feeling their own excitement at the prospect of productivity for America. And in America, productivity is normal. Let’s get to it.

Photo from Adobe Stock The roughly 26,000 Vermonters who receive their health insurance through the state employees’ plan will see a 9% increase in their healthcare premiums starting Jan. 1, according to a memo from the Vermont Department Human Resources. This increase matches last year’s 9% raise, which followed steep, double-digit increases between 2023-2025, according to Ted Fisher, a spokesperson for the state’s Department of Human Resources. He said that this year’s rates are a hopeful signal that Vermont has “turned the corner on the trend in annual increases for our state employees.” He is hopeful that it means next year could see a “lower or no increase next year.” Still, the state employees’ union has used the announcement as an opportunity to call on the governor to fast track price caps on hospital care for those on the state employee plans. In June, Gov. Phil Scott vetoed the Legislature’s effort to implement this kind of price cap for school employees and Affordable Care Act marketplace plans. “I think the governor needs to really put reforming the healthcare system at the forefront of his agenda,” Steve Howard, executive director of the Vermont State Employees’ Association, the union representing state workers, told VTDigger. Though Vermont is in the process of putting price caps on hospital prices for all commercial health insurance in the state, the union is urging Scott to sign an executive order to implement these lower prices tied to a benchmarked price of what Medicare pays for the service for state employees. Montana established this type of reference-based pricing for its state employees’ health plans in 2016, but has since sunset it . Oklahoma, South Carolina , West Virginia and eight other states have some version of the price caps for public employee health plans. Vermont is unique among states in its emphasis on price caps across the entire commercial market . READ MORE Scott supports the price caps for all payers, not just a subset of insurance plans, his spokesperson Amanda Wheeler told VTDigger, adding that the governor signed the broad reference-based pricing plan into law. It’s the same reasoning he gave for vetoing this spring’s attempt to fast-track the plan first for public schools’ and marketplace plans. “Implementing it for just one subset of the insurance market would mean other Vermonters would be excluded from those affordability gains, while adding further complexity, inequity, and cost to an already complicated healthcare system,” Wheeler wrote in an email. A 2024 report by the independent healthcare regulator that was ultimately tasked with implementing Vermont’s reference based pricing plan, analyzed the impact a price cap for hospital charges could have on public school employees’ and state employees’ healthcare plans. They found that if the state kept hospital charges for those plans at two times Medicare rates — rather than the status quo of an average 289% of Medicare’s charges — the state could have prevented $400 million of claims payments during the five-year study period. In 2022 alone, the cap could have cut $79 million. Health insurance, broadly, is a measure of the cost of services times the number of services used. Less costly hospital claims means the insurer needs to collect less in premiums to cover them, which means the state would pay less to cover those premiums. For the VSEA plans, the state covers 80% of employees’ premiums. In 2027, the least expensive plans available to state employees have a monthly price tag of $747 for an individual, $1,494 for two people and $2,054 for a family of three or more. “That eats into people’s wages at a time when — because of the president’s tariffs and the economy and the price of gas and the war in Iran and all that stuff — it’s harder and harder for state employees to make ends meet,” Howard said. The increase comes as other insurance groups across Vermont are starting to see the impacts of efforts to lower costs. In August, plans sold on the state’s Affordable Care Act exchange received some of the smallest increases they’ve ever had. That’s due to reduced hospital budgets, reductions in BlueCross BlueShield’s 2026 contract with the state’s largest hospital network, and a 2025 law that capped the cost of some expensive drugs. The same forces influenced Vermont public school employees’ health insurance plans , which expect to see some of the smallest premium increases in more than a decade. Fisher, with the state’s human resources department, said that the state employees’ plans are on track to follow those trends. Before the pandemic, the plans had very small annual increases, he said, but following it, they saw a “spike” in claims and utilization — which is not uncommon as many people went without optional care during the height of COVID-19. That spike pushed the state employee medical fund into a deficit, he said, which $18.5 million of FY25 state general funds have worked to stabilize. This year’s rates seek to do the same kind of stabilization. “As a result of this money and utilization rates stabilizing, we anticipate the fund being in surplus by the end of FY28 (barring unforeseen economic/healthcare factors),” Fisher added. items.originalTitle: Elon Musk’s SpaceX is betting $74 billion on AI data centers. Texas and Arizona want to know who pays for the power
items.author: Heather Occhino
items.title: Elon Musk’s SpaceX is betting $74 billion on AI data centers. Texas and Arizona want to know who pays for the power
items.summary: SpaceX wants to build a data center in the Arizona desert that would draw 6,000 megawatts of power at full build-out. That is nearly two-thirds of the all-time peak demand that Arizona Public Service, which serves about 1.5 million homes and businesses, hit across its entire system this summer, according to KJZZ . The Cochise County campus is the larger half of a plan SpaceX announced on Nov. 12 to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing sites: roughly $50 billion in southeastern Arizona and more than $24 billion at Starbase, Texas, Reuters reported . The company is pitching both as projects that pay for themselves, with on-site power in Texas, dry cooling in Arizona, and promises of lower bills and taxes for neighbors. Residents, local officials, and now Arizona’s attorney general want proof first. Who covers the cost of the power plants, water, and grid upgrades behind AI, the company or the people who live next door, is quickly becoming the question that decides whether these campuses get built. The stakes for SpaceX are large. Its AI segment produced more than half of its third-quarter revenue, ahead of rockets and Starlink, according to Reuters, and Fortune has reported on how renting out computing capacity to Anthropic and Google has become central to the company’s valuation. The political ground is shifting under the industry, too: voters sided against data center development in 37 of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts this month, as Fortune reported after the midterms . In Texas, a land swap puts the project past a moratorium The Texas campus is a gas-fired power plant and “super-compute facility” on 444.45 acres near the Port of Brownsville, The Texas Tribune reported . Brownsville de-annexed the land earlier this year at SpaceX’s request, after the company offered $220 million for city water and wastewater projects. The neighboring city of Starbase, which incorporated around SpaceX’s launch site in 2025, then annexed it. That sequence leaves the project outside the reach of Brownsville’s 90-day data center moratorium, which took effect in early November. The city says its decision was based on the “information and circumstances presented at the time.” Because the plant would generate its own electricity, SpaceX says the facility won’t draw from the public grid. It will still burn a lot of gas. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued an air permit on Nov. 16 that allows 35 natural gas turbines producing 750 megawatts and up to 248 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, Newsweek reported , citing Politico . The South Texas Environmental Justice Network has announced a protest, arguing the facilities would pollute the air, use up water, and raise residents’ energy bills. Other residents see opportunity. “There’s a lot of people that need jobs in our community and SpaceX has contributed to those jobs,” Janie Melendez, a Brownsville school teacher who previously served on the Texas Republican Party’s executive committee, told the Tribune . Melendez has felt SpaceX’s pull in another way. “Since SpaceX moved in, my home has tripled in value,” she said. Rising values are a win for owners, but they tend to lift property tax bills and rents, which can squeeze newer residents and renters. The tax question is now live. On Nov. 17, Cameron County commissioners voted 3-2 against moving ahead with talks on a 10-year, 100% property tax abatement for the project. Starbase’s own city commission is scheduled to consider a tax abatement on Dec. 9. And in January, SpaceX will face a new governor, Gina Hinojosa, who has vowed to freeze data center approvals until lawmakers pass new protections. In Arizona, a 6-gigawatt campus tests a rural grid The Arizona campus would sit on 747 acres near the Willcox Playa, about 80 miles east of Tucson, according to the Arizona Daily Star . It would take power from the grid through the Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative and the Arizona Electric Power Cooperative, and SpaceX says the nearby Apache Generating Station, which burns coal and natural gas, would grow from about 1 gigawatt to more than 6 gigawatts. The permit application lists $3.6 billion in planned grid upgrades. SpaceX’s pitch to the county is aggressive. At a community meeting, Riley Trettle, who heads SpaceX’s energy and supercomputer department, said the project would reduce residents’ electricity bills, lower property taxes by 20%, and create about 1,000 permanent jobs, according to the Star . The application projects a one-time $250 million sales tax benefit for the county and $35 million to $103 million in sales tax revenue, and the company expects about 5,500 construction jobs. Water is the sharper worry. The campus would be dry-cooled and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, though an existing well could supply up to 10 acre-feet a year for drinking water and maintenance. Residents point to an aquifer already drawn down by large dairy farms, and experts told the Star that the water used to generate the campus’s power could raise annual data center water use by 60% to 90%. The permit doesn’t estimate that figure. On Nov. 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission to postpone its Dec. 9 vote until state and federal agencies can review the project. Her letter questions how SpaceX would cover power needs beyond what the regional cooperative can generate, and raises concerns about water, fire safety, traffic, wildlife, and nearby Fort Huachuca. “The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude,” Mayes said in a statement . She plans her own town hall at Cochise Elementary School on Dec. 3. Is growth paying for growth? Arizona’s larger utilities are already wrestling with the same cost split. APS describes its approach as “growth pays for growth”: large customers sign long-term contracts so they, rather than residential and small commercial customers, cover the infrastructure they require, Scripps News reported . Data centers accounted for about 7% of APS’s peak load this year, up from about 5% last year, according to KJZZ . Regulators draw a finer line. Arizona Corporation Commissioner Kevin Thompson says data centers will pay for any new generation they require, but all customers should share reliability investments that benefit the whole grid. “If it’s for the betterment of the grid as a whole, then that peanut butter should be spread across the bread, right?” he told KJZZ. Meanwhile, APS is asking the commission to approve a 14% to 16% rate increase for residential customers. In that case, an APS witness, Jamie Moe, acknowledged that residential demand isn’t causing high growth-related costs, KJZZ reported. SpaceX’s Arizona campus would be served by cooperatives rather than APS, but any rate increase would still need the Corporation Commission’s approval. The Dec. 9 votes in Starbase and Cochise County will be the first public tests of whether SpaceX’s promise that its AI campuses will pay their own way holds up once the bills, and the gigawatts, come due. items.originalTitle: Jeff Bezos donated $198.9 million in Amazon stock in two days, including shares he’s held since 1994
items.author: Bilin Lin
items.title: Jeff Bezos donated $198.9 million in Amazon stock in two days, including shares he’s held since 1994
items.summary: Jeff Bezos gave away nearly $200 million worth of Amazon stock over two days this month, bringing his disclosed charitable stock donations this year to more than $600 million. The Amazon founder and executive chair donated 674,088 shares on Nov. 12 and another 97,404 shares the following day, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Nov. 16. Forbes valued the 771,492 shares at $198.9 million based on Amazon’s closing price that day of $257.75. The Bezos Earth Fund Foundation, which Bezos founded, received the smaller gift, worth about $25 million, and filed a notice of its intent to sell the shares . Bezos acquired those shares on July 5, 1994, the day he incorporated the company that became Amazon and nearly three years before its 1997 IPO. The gifts come with the Earth Fund’s deadline about four years away. Bezos launched the fund in 2020 with a pledge to give away $10 billion by 2030. As of late September it had granted about $2.4 billion, meaning it would need to average roughly $1.8 billion a year to hit the target, Fortune reported . Where the shares went The November gifts follow two earlier rounds. Bezos donated more than 1.25 million Amazon shares in May and 415,580 shares in August , worth about $323 million and $107 million, respectively, at the Nov. 16 close. Altogether, Bezos has donated at least 2.44 million Amazon shares this year, worth approximately $629.1 million at that price. Day 1 Academies, the nonprofit that runs Bezos Academy, his network of tuition-free preschools, received at least 450,837 of those shares: 220,200 in May and 230,637 in August. Together, the two nonprofits he founded account for about 22.5% of this year’s donated shares. The filings describe the rest as gifts to nonprofits without naming the recipients. Even after the donations, Bezos directly held more than 878 million shares of Amazon, No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 , valued at approximately $226.4 billion as of the Nov. 16 close, per Forbes . This year’s gifts amount to less than 0.3% of that stake. What the two known recipients do On Nov. 19, the Earth Fund told Fortune exclusively that it was committing more than $100 million to protect the Amazon rainforest through 15 new grants across South America. Cristián Samper, the fund’s managing director and leader for nature solutions, said it would use grantee reports and independent satellite analysis to track whether forests remain standing and deforestation declines. Day 1 Academies runs 38 tuition-free, Montessori-inspired preschools in underserved communities across Arizona, Florida, Hawaii, Kentucky, Texas, and Washington. It enrolled 2,456 students for the 2026–27 school year, according to its annual report . The preschools grew out of the $2 billion philanthropic commitment Bezos announced in 2018 to support early childhood education and families experiencing homelessness. Through the other arm of that commitment, the Day 1 Families Fund , Bezos funds local organizations that help families move from shelters or the streets into stable housing. In 2025, the fund awarded $102.5 million to 32 groups in 20 states, the District of Columbia, and Guam. How much has Bezos given away? Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos, had given away an estimated $4.7 billion through the end of 2025, placing them 10th on Forbes ’ list of America’s top philanthropists . Forbes put their giving at about $600 million in 2025. Bezos told CNN in 2022 that he planned to give away most of his fortune during his lifetime. He said “the hard part is figuring out how to do it in a levered way,” drawing a comparison to building Amazon. “So we’re building the capacity to be able to give away this money,” he said. His ex-wife, MacKenzie Scott, whose net worth Forbes estimated at $27.1 billion as of Nov. 20, gave away $7.2 billion in 2025 alone . That brought her total since her 2019 divorce from Bezos to $26.4 billion, according to Forbes . That single year of giving was more than Bezos and Sánchez Bezos have donated over their lifetimes. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: This 71-year-old cattleman’s farm brings in $30 million a year. He says the cattle cycle that built it is broken
items.author: Mia Osmonbekov
items.title: This 71-year-old cattleman’s farm brings in $30 million a year. He says the cattle cycle that built it is broken
items.summary: Cows have roamed Will Harris’s 3,200-acre home farm in southwestern Georgia since 1866, when his great-grandparents got up at dawn six days a week to tend the land. They raised and slaughtered chickens, ducks, hogs, and cows, and would load up the meat in a mule-drawn wagon and drive it up the two-mile dirt road to the town of Bluffton, which had a population of 117 people at the last census, to peddle. Now Harris, 71, has grown its operations into White Oak Pastures , a 5,700-acre farming ecosystem that he told Fortune is the largest private employer in the county and employs 170 people, almost everyone in Bluffton who isn’t retired or can’t work for other reasons. White Oak’s workforce is larger than the town itself. “Just about everybody in town that works, works for us,” Harris said. His business, which raises livestock, processes the meat and sells it directly to consumers, brings in $30 million a year. But Harris says the cycle that built farms like his has broken. Record cattle prices once would have sent ranchers rushing to rebuild their herds. Now the land to do it costs more than cattle can pay for, as investors and developers outbid farmers across rural Georgia. So instead of expanding, he is training new ranchers and is open to a data center coming to his county, because he isn’t sure the old way of building a farm still works. “I don’t know how this is going to end,” he said. The U.S. cattle herd is at a 75-year low due to droughts and record-high operating costs, and the price of ground beef, typically the most affordable part of the animal for consumers, hit a record $6.90 per pound earlier this year . Farmland is also harder to buy as farmers are outbid by institutional investors and developers, including the data center companies spreading across rural Georgia . Harris said a data center was approved for construction in his Clay County, but hasn’t started construction. “If you can get a tremendous amount of money to sell the land, most people sell it. It happens every day, and it’s not just data centers,” Harris said. “The land is moving out of the hands of the farmer or cattle producers into the hands of others.” Courtesy of White Oak Pastures Living through the ups and downs of the cattle industry White Oak wasn’t always run the way it is now, which is as a regenerative farm, a concept Harris defines as “not breaking the cycles of nature.” When Harris’s father inherited the farm after World War II, he got rid of everything except for cattle and started selling calves to feedlots instead of slaughtering and delivering meat himself, using pesticides and chemical fertilizers to cut costs. Harris went to college and studied animal science, then returned to run the farm similarly for 20 years until 1995. “I wanted nothing in my pastures except cattle and Tifton 85 Bermuda grass, and if you were not a cow or Tifton 85 Bermuda grass, I would kill you,” he said. “I went to my pastures every single day with the focus of looking for something to kill.” But then he saw how hard this was on the animals and the land, and changed his approach to reflect “the very old-fashioned way of farming” of his great-grandparents—raising cattle alongside sheep, pigs, goats, and poultry; dropping pesticides; and allowing in more types of grasses. “It was not easy, but I went from raising cattle very industrially to raising cattle in a very natural manner,” he said. “Now, when I go to the pastures, I’m looking for how to keep everything alive and prospering.” The shift paid off in the early 2000s, when Harris said “the messaging for grass-fed beef” became more widespread and shoppers started looking for it. That let him put his beef on shelves at Whole Foods and Publix , since the four meatpackers that control 85% of U.S. beef supply had little of it. He said sales grew to about $25 million in 2015, and then the U.S. changed its country-of-origin labeling rules for beef, opening the door for imported beef from places like Australia, Brazil, and Argentina processed or packaged in the U.S. to carry a “Product of USA” label. While Harris kept selling the same volume of beef, his business became unprofitable because he had to cut prices to compete. “We went from being quite profitable to not being profitable because of that change, and I had a few rough years,” he said. That changed this year. Since Jan. 1, the USDA has reserved the “Product of USA” label for meat from animals born, raised, slaughtered and processed in the U.S. The pandemic had already given White Oak a new path. The big meatpackers had to shutter some operations, but also Harris’s daughter came home from college and launched White Oak’s online store with which they could sell directly to customers instead of going through the grocery stores. Harris even opened his first physical store in Atlanta this year, though he has no further plans of expansion. “We want to do better, not bigger,” he said. Supporting the next generation of farmers Harris is teaching other farmers to do what he does. He said most industrial farmers can’t easily switch to regenerative methods because they’ve already invested so much into equipment—saying a cotton picker costs about $1.4 million and a grain combine nearly $1 million—and like him, learned how to do it from their predecessors. “I don’t want to make it sound like I’m doing it right and they’re not and they’re bad people,” he said. “These farmers are doing it the way they learned from their granddad and dad, the way they learned at the land grant university.” His nonprofit, the Center for Agricultural Resilience, takes six interns per quarter for three months on the farm, and White Oak offers jobs to about half of them. Harris also runs week-long courses on raising cattle and hogs about once a month, drawing 25 to 30 people from across the country and even from England, Spain, Germany, and Mexico. “They’re frequently young people that are just out of college, or maybe they’ve taken an entry-level job and didn’t like it,” he said. “There are some people who have inherited farms at 30, 40, 50 years of age, and then they come, so it’s all over the board.” He said counties like his own in Georgia once thrived on farming, but since World War II, companies like Tyson and Cargill took a bigger share of the profits from agriculture, leaving less for those communities. This is why he’s more open to data centers despite having concerns, though he said he’s not part of the opposition because he doesn’t know enough yet. “These agricultural counties in southwest Georgia are economically impoverished, and we need some other things going on,” he said. “I don’t know if data centers are what we need, but it is some initial relief, and we will see how it goes.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.title: Harvard scientist may never prove mysterious space object’s origin after mission scrapped
items.summary: A Harvard astrophysicist who claims a mysterious object speeding through our solar system is actually a lost Soviet spacecraft says scientists may never be able to get a clear look at it after Japan abruptly scrapped a planned mission to land on the target. Avi Loeb told Fox News Digital that the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's decision to cancel its 2031 Hayabusa2 rendezvous with the object known as 1998 KY26 removes the only opportunity to capture high-resolution images of its surface and settle whether it is a natural space rock or the missing 1988 Soviet probe Phobos 1. "There is no way by which we can actually resolve the object, or get a high-resolution image of its surface, without coming close to it — without a flyby — because even with the Webb telescope or the biggest telescopes we have on Earth, the object is not close enough to be resolved into multiple pixels in an image," Loeb said. MYSTERIOUS OBJECT MOVING THROUGH SPACE COULD BE LOST SOVIET PROBE AS NASA WEIGHS IN ON THEORY The cancellation came just days after NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman dismissed speculation about the roughly 36-foot-wide object during an appearance on "Fox & Friends," saying, "I've not seen any evidence to suggest this is ... anything other than an asteroid." Loeb pushed back on that assessment, arguing KY26 is "not an asteroid" because it accelerates in a way gravity alone cannot explain and predicting that when Japan's spacecraft lands on it in July 2031, scientists would find a label reading "Made in the USSR" instead of ice or rock. NASA CHIEF CONFIRMS AGENCY HAS UNEXPLAINED UFO IMAGERY: 'WE DON'T KNOW WHAT IT IS' Japan's space agency reported to the Cabinet Office's Space Policy Committee on Nov. 16 that it was abandoning the 2031 rendezvous after the last normally functioning main ion engine on Hayabusa2 malfunctioned in mid-August, according to the Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun. "I was surprised that the cancellation by JAXA occurred just a day or two after I spoke about it publicly, because the malfunction in the engine was known for several months," Loeb said. "The probability that we're dealing with a coincidence where within a day after my public discourse, JAXA decides to cancel this mission is a day divided by the duration over which it was known that the fourth engine is malfunctioning – and that was over 100 days or so. TRUMP HIGHLIGHTS NASA NUCLEAR-POWERED MARS SPACECRAFT MISSION PLANNED FOR 2028 "So, I would argue that the probability for a chance coincidence is less than 1%, but it could still be a coincidence," he added. Loeb noted that Hayabusa2 was designed over several years and questioned why Japanese engineers did not attempt an Earth gravity-assist maneuver to compensate for the lost engine thrust rather than pivoting to another target. JAXA officials said in their report that reaching KY26 in 2031 already required an Earth gravity assist, and that combining working parts from two damaged engines left the 12-year-old spacecraft without enough thrust to perform the necessary orbital changes, prompting a redirect to a 2028 flyby of asteroid 2015 BM510 instead, the newspaper added. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Even without a close-up flyby, Loeb said astronomers still have one major tool left to test his theory from afar by using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to measure the heat radiating off KY26 and analyze its chemical spectrum. SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POTENTIALLY MASSIVE DWARF PLANET CANDIDATE HIDING BEYOND PLUTO "So far, we detected a reflection of sunlight from this object, but the Webb telescope can potentially detect the heat emitted by the object, and that will offer us an opportunity to learn both about the size, the surface temperature of the object, as well as the composition of the object," Loeb said. While mainstream scientists have suggested KY26 is an ordinary rock or comet, Loeb noted the object rotates about once every five minutes and is far brighter than expected. EIFFEL TOWER-SIZED ASTEROID APOPHIS TO PASS CLOSER TO EARTH THAN MANY SATELLITES IN 2029, NASA SAYS SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS "This object reflects about half of the sunlight that is impinging on it, whereas a typical rock or iceberg reflects about 5% of the sunlight impinging on it," Loeb said, adding that the object's brightness is "surprising." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB NASA previously told Fox News Digital that a 2025 orbital study led by the agency's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies concluded KY26's complex trajectory is driven by solar radiation forces – "the natural push of sunlight and thermal emission on its non-spherical shape" – rather than hidden comet-like activity. SEND US A TIP Loeb and his colleagues, however, found KY26's trajectory closely resembles that of Phobos 1 – a Soviet spacecraft launched toward Mars in July 1988 that shut down after a faulty command – and calculated that sunlight reflecting off its solar panels could produce the observed push without any signs of a "dark comet" tail. GOT A TIP? "It could be a comet shedding some gas backward that is pushing it forward, but in that case we should have seen the gas," Loeb said. "We should have seen the dust because for comets we see a tail and the dust particles are being pushed away from the sun by the solar radiation." TRUMP SAYS AIR FORCE PILOTS DESCRIBED A ROUND UFO FLYING THREE TIMES FASTER THAN AN F-22 FIGHTER JET LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Loeb added that KY26 orbits the sun at a distance of a fraction to a few times the separation between Earth and the sun and poses no threat of hitting Earth, though he argued space agencies must remain open-minded when tracking unexplained objects. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL He noted that in January 2025, astronomers briefly cataloged an object near Earth as an asteroid before realizing it was actually the Tesla Roadster launched into space by SpaceX in 2018 – a mistake that was only caught because humans knew its flight path. "Hopefully, the Rubin Observatory in Chile that is funded by the Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation will find dozens of interstellar objects in the coming decade, and we should be curious enough to check whether all of them are rocks or icebergs, because if one of them is technological in origin, that will change our view on our place in the universe," Loeb said.
