items.title: MAGA’s cool factor faces a test as Dallas Young Republicans confront midterm defeats
items.summary: Is it still cool to be MAGA? Dallas Young Republicans weighed in. After Republican losses across the country in the 2026 midterm elections , young adults came together Tuesday to discuss what happened and how to move forward. Fox News Digital spoke with attendees and members about where they stand on the MAGA movement. Chad Cohen, the president of Dallas Young Republicans (DYR), is confident that it is still cool to be MAGA. "One hundred percent," Cohen said. "I think I speak for all of my members when I say we're still totally behind President Donald Trump . The MAGA movement is still early, it's still young." AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Cohen said the movement is looking for more politicians, like Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, Rep.-elect Jace Yarbrough, R-Texas, and Vice-President JD Vance . However, not all members share Cohen's feelings. DYR member Mark said he is "on the fence." "I'm a three-time Trump voter, but starting the new war with Iran was kind of a big letdown with this election," he said. Ethan shared a very blunt assessment of the election and said the Republican Party needs to go in a different direction than MAGA. "I would honestly say no at this point," he said. "I think in the 2026 midterm elections, Trump asked the people to come out and vote as if he was on the ballot, and people did. The 2026 midterms were a refutation of Trump." DYR member Dan said whether or not it is still cool to be MAGA depends on "what your definition of MAGA is." "I think after the midterms, we've seen some fragmentation within our party, which is part of the reason why we lost," he said. "I think people view there being two major factions, the MAGA party versus the American First Party. So I think our job as young Republicans here in one of the most conservative cities in the country to try to find a way to mobilize young people. To believe in the same vision that brought us together back in 2016." VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY Jack still believes it is cool to be MAGA. "I think so," he said. "A lot of young men that run around in my crowd, I mean, we obviously still vote Republican, but I think a little bit of the young vote may have been lost due to social media, what's on there nowadays." Jack added that the war in Iran was a big issue. "I think the Iran war was a really big one ... impact to the MAGA message. I think that what it stands for at its core, especially like in the first term, what MAGA meant to us back then and what I voted for back then, I think it's still cool. I mean, in my circles, I think, it's true 100 percent." Matthew Monfore, a political consultant and advisor who has spent time speaking to college students, doesn't think it is considered cool to be MAGA anymore based on what he has heard. "Apparently not, what I'm seeing among conservatives on college campuses," he said. TRUMP'S IRAN GAMBLE DIVIDES GOP HAWKS AND 'AMERICA FIRST' CONSERVATIVES OVER WHAT VICTORY LOOKS LIKE Matthew said that supporting MAGA is neither good nor bad. "I think at the heart of it, Make America Great Again was putting Americans first," he said. "And I think through the midterms, I think that a lot of people strayed away from putting Americans first as an American. I don't know if it's still considered to be good or bad. I think it's just at the heart of it, I think Republicans strayed away from putting the American party first." Kai agreed that Make America Great Again is centered on putting America first. "I think there's been a lot of hardships that we've all had to deal with just at a global scale, but when it comes down to the American people, I think putting the American first, especially from here on out," Kai said. "I think it's very important and I think that we can all be better for it if we choose to do so."

She declared, while at a Welsh denim factory last year, that she 'loves making things,' referring to knitting and sewing." William and Kate want their children to grow up with a sense of normalcy. Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that the couple's down-to-earth approach reflects the kind of royal family they believe the British public wants to see. "And the children do chores at the same time. William makes sure that they understand exactly what life is like in modern-day Britain. So, the children will do things like gardening.
